name: Korean shamanism
info: Korean shamanism, known as Musok or Muism, is the polytheistic folk religion of Korea, centred on gods and ancestral spirits and on ritual specialists called mudang; its earliest historical references date to the 12th century.

facts.origin: Korea; the origins are unclear and the earliest historical references to mudang date to the 12th century, though Musok is often perceived as ancient.
facts.founder: none: there is no central authority and no single founder; Korean origin myths name the first mudang as the eight daughters of Bupŭ-Whasang or as granddaughters of a princess, and legend makes Tan'gun the national ancestor and first mudang.
facts.scriptures: none written: Musok has no doctrine and is orally transmitted; mudang inherit their chants (muga) and recite origin myths (ponp'uri) in rituals.
facts.followers: Over 200,000 mudang in South Korea in the early 21st century, members of professional organisations; a late 20th-century Korean Gallup survey found that 38 percent of South Korean adults had used a mudang; Religious Intelligence puts about 16 percent of North Koreans as practising "traditional ethnic" religion.

t: Musok is a polytheistic religion without doctrine or central authority, in which ritual specialists called mudang, most of them women, mediate between people and the gods and ancestral spirits.
The mudang's central ritual is the gut, a performance of rhythmic movement, song, oracles and offerings in which the spirits are entertained and, through the mudang, speak directly to the living.

Suppressed under the Joseon dynasty, by modernisers, by the Japanese and by South Korean governments, Musok has since the late 1970s been increasingly seen as a source of Korean cultural identity, though the mudang remain widely stigmatised.
dyk: Mudang say that the gods choose them: a person who resists the calling may be tormented with misfortune, illness or madness, called sinbyŏng, until they accept it and are trained by an established mudang.
ev: The term mu is first recorded in Korea, in the Yisanggugjip and the Samguk sagi, which describe spirit mediumship, exorcism, divination and ancestor veneration
Images of Musok deities are first recorded
In an extreme case of the persecution of mudang under the Joseon dynasty, a mudang is beheaded
Jeju governor Yi Hyŏngsang purges the island's simbang and destroys 129 shrines
Police launch a crackdown, arresting mudang, destroying shrines and burning paraphernalia
The Japanese colonial government launches the Mind Cultivation Movement, among its measures to suppress Musok
The Saemaul Undong, or New Community Movement, brings a surge in police suppression of mudang in South Korea, and they form a federation to promote their interests
The Yŏngdŭng gut performed at Ch'ilmŏri Shrine on Jeju is added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

sections.origins:
Korean shamanism, also called Musok (무속) or Muism (무교), is a religion from Korea. Its origins are unclear: it is often perceived as ancient, but the scholar Jung Young Lee calls them "almost impossible" to trace, since detailed accounts of mudang rituals before the modern period are rare and the tradition is orally transmitted. Prehistoric Koreans, like other Northeast Asian peoples, had a religion that venerated spirits, animals and celestial bodies, and some historians argue that Musok shares a prehistoric origin with other North Asian traditions sometimes labelled "shamanic". The historian Richard McBride cautions that the word "shamanism" does not do justice to the sources for ancient Korean religions.

The term mu was adopted from Chinese. It is first recorded in Korea in the 12th-century Yisanggugjip and appears again in the 12th-century Samguk sagi. Eleven references to the practices of mu appear in Korean historical records of the 12th and 13th centuries, five of them from the northern kingdom of Koguryŏ, and they indicate spirit mediumship, exorcism, divination and ancestor veneration; further accounts describe mu in the southern kingdoms of Paekche and Silla. The term mudang arose later. Over time the mudang's practices absorbed many elements from Buddhism, Confucianism and Daoism.

Korean myths tell of the first mudang. In one tale they were the eight daughters of Bupŭ-Whasang, who went out in different directions and spread the tradition through Korea; the number eight likely refers to the country's eight traditional provinces. Other stories name an ancient princess as the founder, among them Pari-Kongchu in the Seoul area and Gongsim in Gyeongsang Province.
sections.beliefs:
Musok is polytheistic. Its supernatural beings are called gwisin or sin, and the mudang divide them into gods and ancestral spirits. The gwisin are deemed volatile: they bring good fortune to those who do well by them, and offended they can bring suffering. Devotees believe they can converse and bargain with them. More than 130 Musok divinities have been identified. Some embody natural or cosmological forces, among them the mountain god sansin, usually pictured as a white-bearded man with a tiger, and the dragon kings of rivers and seas; others were once human, including monarchs, officials and generals. The highest god, Hananim, is thought to rule the heavens but is rarely worshipped. Many deities want food, drink, song and dance, and receive them as offerings.

Households have their own deities, the chief of whom is Sŏngju, the principal house guardian, and villages traditionally had Jangseung posts as guardians. Ancestral spirits are called chosang. Musok rites, unlike the Confucian jesa, let ancestors speak directly to the living, and they include ancestors that the patrilineal rites leave out. Mountains, rocks, springs and trees are held to be places of spiritual power, and Mount Paektu is held to be the most sacred mountain.

According to Korean traditional belief, after death a soul stands trial and passes through gates kept by the Ten Kings. Spirits of those who died tragically or too soon may wander the human world as jabkwi and bring affliction to the living, and the mudang are often thought the best specialists to find out what such ghosts want and send them away.
sections.texts:
Musok has no scripture and no doctrine, and it is passed on orally. Its stories are the origin myths called ponp'uri, which Korean scholars have extensively collected and studied. A mudang recites them during a ritual, in full at a longer one or in condensed form at a shorter one, and the recitation is deemed to add to the ritual's efficacy. The story of Princess Pari is commonly recited during gut for the dead.

The language of a gut is called mudang sori, "mudang's sounds", and is often deliberately archaic. The songs or chants are called muga. Each practitioner has a personal repertoire, largely inherited through oral tradition, and some mudang have also sung pop songs to entertain the spirits. Incantations for communicating with a spirit are called chukeon.

Paintings of the deities, called musindo, are another record of the faith's imagery. They are particularly important in the Musok of Seoul and of the northwestern provinces of Hwanghae and P'yŏngan, and they use colours associated with the five directions: red, blue or green, yellow, white and black. The earliest evidence for images of the deities is from the 13th century. Painters traditionally bathed beforehand and refrained from eating fish or meat. A painting is regarded as a seat for the deity, literally manifesting its presence. Since the 1970s musindo have commonly been made in commercial workshops, and since the 1980s and 1990s they have become collectable.

The words "Korean shamanism" and Musok are themselves modern scholarly labels. Musok was coined by the folklorist Yi Nŭnghwa, and "shamanism" came into English studies of Korea from the late 19th century.
sections.spread:
The sources for the early history of Musok are thin. The records of the 12th and 13th centuries place mu in the northern kingdom of Koguryŏ and in the southern kingdoms of Paekche and Silla, and compare them with the ritual specialists of northern China. Before Christianity arrived in the 17th and 18th centuries, Korean religion was rarely exclusivist, and many Koreans practised Daoism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Musok at the same time. Musok and Buddhism are especially intertwined: mudang often identify as Buddhists, use incantations from Buddhist sutras and worship Buddhist deities, and some Buddhist temples venerate deities traditionally associated with Musok.

Within Korea the two main kinds of mudang had different homes. The kangsin-mu, who are possessed by deities, were historically more common in the northern and central peninsula, and the hereditary sesŭp-mu in the south below the Han River. The Korean War, the division of Korea and urbanisation moved many people about the peninsula. Many mudang from Hwanghae, in North Korea, resettled in Inchon and strongly influenced Musok there. By the late 20th century the kangsin-mu tradition, with its costumes and paraphernalia, was dominant across South Korea, and by the early 21st century it increasingly prevailed even on Jeju, where the sesŭp-mu had predominated, which has produced rivalry between the two.

Musok is primarily found in South Korea. Since at least the 20th century mudang have travelled abroad to perform rituals, for instance for Japan's Korean minority; there are also mudang in Europe, a small number of non-Koreans have become mudang, and since the 1990s mudang from South Korea have made pilgrimages to Mount Paektu in China.
sections.community:
The mudang are free agents rather than an ordained clergy, and ritual is for them an economic activity. Many depend on it as a full-time job, and modern South Korean practitioners advertise in brochures, newspapers and on the Internet. Most mudang are women, and about a fifth are men; on Jeju there were more male than female simbang before the 1950s. Mudang have conventionally belonged to the lowest social class. In 1983 around 43,000 people belonged to mudang unions, and in the early 21st century more than 200,000 mudang were members of professional organisations, with the highest concentrations in Seoul and on Jeju.

Under the Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) the mudang were persecuted. Confucian elites regarded Musok rites as improper, and mudang belonged to one of eight outcast groups expelled from the capital. The Gyeonggukdaejeon law book prescribed 100 lashes in public for anyone found supporting them, a mudang was beheaded in 1398, and in 1702 the governor of Jeju destroyed 129 shrines. The rites were taxed until the Kabo reforms of 1895, yet the government also turned to mudang in emergencies such as epidemics, droughts and famines. From the late 19th century many modernisers, Christians among them, called Musok misin, "superstition". The Japanese suppressed it after 1910, and in North Korea mudang were labelled part of the "hostile class".

Clients are mostly women, who come with practical troubles such as illness, financial worry or concern for a child, and who often regard themselves as Buddhists or Christians. In South Korea, disapproval of mudang as charlatans remains widespread, especially among Protestants, some of whom harass mudang at work or during ceremonies; the mudang regard this as religious discrimination.
sections.legacy:
The nationalist reimagining of Musok began under Japanese rule. Scholars such as Ch'oe Nam-sŏn and Yi Nŭnghwa in the 1920s presented it as the remnant of an ancient, primordial Korean religion, an idea that mudang themselves later promoted heavily. In the 1970s the spread of folklore studies led to wider acceptance among South Koreans that Musok was Korea's ancient religion. South Korea's Cultural Properties Protection Law of 1962 recognised performing arts as intangible cultural heritage, and some folklorists used it to defend the mudang. From the 1980s the government designated certain mudang as Human Cultural Treasures, among them Kim Kŭm-hwa, who toured Western countries. By 2009 it recognised ten regional gut styles as intangible cultural heritage.

Several mudang joined the minjung pro-democracy movement from the 1970s and became emblematic of its cause. From the 1980s they began writing books about themselves, and portrayals on South Korean film and television moved from showing mudang as harmful and anti-modern, in films of the 1960s and 1970s, to showing Musok as a living tradition in the cities from the mid-2000s. The artist Nam June Paik, who cited Musok as an influence, recreated an exorcism gut in performances from the late 1970s.

Mudang have also performed for public causes: in the early 1990s a feminist group in Seoul sponsored a gut for the aggrieved souls of Korean "comfort women", and since the late 1980s simbang on Jeju have led public lamentations for those killed in the Jeju uprising of 1948. The new visibility has improved the mudang's social image, though museums often stress the folkloric and aesthetic value of Musok over its religious function.

summary: Korean shamanism, or Musok, is a polytheistic folk religion of Korea with no doctrine or central authority, in which ritual specialists called mudang, mostly women, mediate with gods and ancestral spirits through the gut ritual. Long suppressed and stigmatised, it has been seen since the late 1970s as part of Korean cultural identity.

James Huntley Grayson, Korea - A Religious History (Routledge, 2002)
Laurel Kendall, Shamans, Nostalgias and the IMF: South Korean Popular Religion in Motion (University of Hawaii Press, 2009)
Chongho Kim, Korean Shamanism: The Cultural Paradox (Routledge, 2018)
notes: Single source: the Wikipedia article Korean shamanism. Its References section has no entries in the saved text, so references are left empty for the editor.

Start 1100 (circa): the article says only that the earliest historical references to mudang date to the 12th century and that the origins are unclear. The tradition itself is often perceived as ancient; the article does not date it.

The article gives Joseon as 1392 to 1897 in one place and the Kabo reforms of 1895 as the end of the rites' taxation; both are used as written. The Japanese invaded in 1910; the Mind Cultivation Movement is dated 1936.
Beliefs and origin myths (Tan'gun as first mudang, the eight daughters, the princess) are told as the tradition's. Rituals described only as far as the article does.
The Koguryŏ references are in records of the 12th and 13th centuries (eleven in all, five from Koguryŏ), not contemporary with the kingdom.

Faith map: the area years are mine where the article is vague: northern and central peninsula and the southern peninsula from 1100 (the earliest records), Jeju from 1400 (simbang first recorded in the 15th century), Inchon from 1950 (Korean War), Japan from 1900 (the article says 'since at least the 20th century'), Paektu pilgrimages from 1990. The Inwangsan mark is placed in 1910, the start of the occupation, since the article gives no exact year for the Guksadang's move. The origin mark names the peninsula, not a site.
Followers: the article gives no world total. The 38 percent figure is the late 20th-century Gallup survey; Musok is not recorded in the South Korean census.
